Eight AI coding assistants each built a standalone WebXR page that visualizes the Mandelbrot set in a virtual room, from one of two prompts (v0 and v1; v0 for two, v1 for six builds). In phase 1, every page was reviewed blind by three kinds of reviewer (HTML, Transcript and Browser), each scoring six criteria from 1 to 10 plus an overall score. In phase 2, five blind judges, each working from different material (HTML, Transcript, HTML + Transcript, Browser and Browser + HTML), ranked all eight from best to worst. The mean of those ranks is the consensus used below. The judges broadly agree: Top four: the two Opus 5.5 builds, then the two GPT6 Pro builds, in every judge's list. Bottom two: the two Copilot builds, in every list except the transcript judge's.

Exceptions: The browser judge put GPT6-Pro-v1 first and Opus-v1 fourth, based on what a desktop user sees first: the room's polish and the XR-info dialog. The transcript judge put Gemini last, because it shipped a shader that failed to compile and was never verified. Core goal met (30%): a recognisable 3D Mandelbrot set inside a room, reachable on desktop/phone without errors; this is the "done when" condition.
XR readiness, judged from source (20%): a correct session setup (reference-space fallbacks, layer/viewport use, AR alpha, input handling), because no XR device or emulator was available.
Visual quality / wow (20%): v1 asks for this explicitly; for v0 it only counts as polish, so a v0 entry is not marked down for lacking it.
Usability and fallbacks (15%): clear Enter VR/AR behaviour when XR is missing, phone layout, touch/keyboard controls, no native dialogs.

Mathematical depth / exploration (10%): zoom depth, presets/tours, precision. These decide whether the set is explorable or just a static prop.
Prompt fidelity and robustness (5%): v0 must use three.js; "standalone" files should not depend on a CDN; no console errors. 1. G (Opus 5.5 · v1, v1): Raw WebGL2 with perturbation zoom (float64 reference orbit, rebasing): Dive reached 2×10¹⁰ with detail intact. The XR-info dialog explains device support; phone layout is clean; the settings panel is rich. Zoom is shallow (about 187×), and Seahorse renders as a large flat plateau. 4. Browser + HTML judge — summary of tests and approach

I read each index.html. For the bundled builds (B, C, H) I skimmed past the three.js bundle and grepped the minified app code for session setup, input and fallbacks. Before testing I grepped every file for alert/confirm/prompt and found only A, with two calls. In one Chrome tab I loaded each localhost origin and stubbed the native dialogs after every load. I read the console, clicked Enter VR/AR (no XR device, so every candidate's unsupported path was exercised), and used each candidate's controls: presets/tours, dive, palettes, walk/immerse, stereo, orbit by dragging, zoom by wheel. I also tested at a phone-like 446 px width, the window manager's minimum. Deep-zoom claims were checked against on-screen readouts (G 1.96×10¹⁰, H width 3×10⁻⁹). Limits: no WebXR emulator, so XR quality was judged from source; frame rate wasn't measured reliably. Sixteen screenshots are in screenshots/.
Each candidate was judged against its own prompt version, so the v0 entries (C, H) had to use three.js, which both bundle inline.

Works out of the box (30%): a recognisable 3D Mandelbrot in a room must appear on a plain desktop or phone browser without errors, because that is the "Done when" bar.
XR entry and fallback behaviour (20%): what Enter VR/AR does when no XR runtime is present (an honest in-page message, a disabled button, or a usable fallback) predicts how the page behaves on unsupported devices.
Usability and controls (20%): orbit, zoom/dive, presets and discoverable help decide whether a person can actually explore the set.

Visual quality against its prompt (20%): v1 is judged on "wow" effect; v0 is judged on a clear, legible 3D room. Each candidate is held only to its own prompt.
Phone-width layout (10%): the prompt names Android and iOS phones, so the UI must stay usable at about 390 px. 1. H (GPT6 Pro · v1, v1): Polished glowing observatory with contour-traced terrain. Destinations, palette, double-click dive and a rich Controls panel (walk, motion look, sound, gentle motion). Exemplary "XR info" capability dialog. ARIA labels throughout and a clean phone layout. No console errors. 2. C (Opus 5.5 · v0, v0): Convincing room: plinth landscape, wall display with zoom-box minimap, in-world control signage and a tablet panel. Tour, shape and colour modes all work. Honest WebXR status text, no errors, usable at phone width. 3.

G (GPT6 Pro · v0, v0): Elegant observatory with clickable complex-plane minimap, destinations, palettes, detail levels, walk mode and a Cardboard-style stereo fallback.
Disabled "VR unavailable" button, strong accessibility labels and a responsive phone UI. Its terrain is less striking than C's, and WASD did nothing in my test. 4. A (Opus 5.5 · v1, v1): Striking pedestal landscape with live Julia-set inset, click-to-dive, auto-dive to Seahorse Valley and progressive refinement. Clear "no WebXR" message. The "Immerse" mode gave confusing camera views, and the toolbar overflows at phone width. 5. D (Gemini 4 Argon · v1, v1): Most features: terrain/Mandelbulb/canyon modes, fly-to presets, sliders, D-pad and a toast on failed VR. The Mandelbulb is the wow moment, but the terrain is noisy and aliased, the phone UI covers the scene, and it depends on the Tailwind CDN. 6.

E (Mistral Large 4 · v1, v1): Recognisable cardioid landscape once orbited, but the default view sees a tilted sheet edge-on, the info panel faces away (mirrored), there is no VR/AR button, and the "needs secure context" hint is wrong on localhost. 7. Browser judge — summary of tests and approach

I loaded each candidate in its own origin in a single Chrome tab I created (closed at the end) and read the console after a fresh reload. I clicked every start button and toolbar control and tried the main presets, palettes, dive/zoom, orbit by drag, scroll zoom and keyboard where offered. On each I pressed Enter VR/AR (or the equivalent) to see the no-XR behaviour. For B I also hid navigator.xr to simulate a non-XR browser, and the fallback still did not appear. Mean rank derived mean = (r 1 + … + r n ) / n over the n judges that ranked the candidate (a judge that did not rank it is left out). Shown to one decimal. Equal means are shown as ties; the place is a competition rank (1, 1, 3, …). Worked example for Opus 5.5 · v1 : ranks 1, 2, 1, 4, 1 → mean = 9 / 5 = 1.8; spread 1–4; σ = 1.17. Spread and σ derived spread = min(r) to max(r) · σ = √( Σ (r i − mean)² / n ) σ is the population standard deviation of the candidate's ranks: 0 means every judge agreed; larger values mean the judges disagreed more.

Kendall τ b derived τ b = (C − D) / √( (C + D + T a ) · (C + D + T b ) ) for two judges, over every pair of candidates both ranked: C = pairs ordered the same way, D = pairs ordered oppositely, T a /T b = pairs tied in only one judge's ranking. +1 = identical order, 0 = unrelated, −1 = reversed. The page makes a stylish first impression, but the Mandelbrot set it is about is almost invisible: decorative glowing ribbons dominate the 3D scene, and the fractal is a faint speckle.
